children: By Joyu Wang
KAOHSIUNG, Taiwan — Ever since former U.S. Navy flight officer Paul Lwin founded defense startup HavocAI in Rhode Island in 2024, he has seen Taiwan as an island of opportunity.
Lwin designs software to manage autonomous maritime fleets — the kind of drone defense that Taiwanese military planners dream of as they assemble deterrence against a Chinese invasion.
"If we can help Taiwan build thousands of these autonomous boats, it could protect Taiwan," he said. "It could prevent a war from breaking out."
American drone-tech startups like HavocAI are swarming into Taiwan and — with the encouragement of U.S. government matchmakers — finding partners who can help them turn blueprints into reality.

The emerging industry has the potential to serve the U.S. military's demand for a secure drone supply chain that steers clear of China, while providing Taiwan with an arsenal that it sees as essential to its survival as a self-ruled democracy.

U.S. startups working with Taiwan on sea and air drones range from small defense-tech firms to Anduril Industries, an arms supplier to the Pentagon and the Taiwan military whose drone contracts with Taipei have already passed the $1 billion mark. At least 13 U.S.-Taiwan collaboration agreements have been signed since September 2025.

For the U.S., making drones on American soil is a policy priority. "Our overt preference is to buy American," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last year as he introduced Drone Dominance, a $1.1 billion Pentagon program to purchase small, lethal drones.

However, "not everything can be made in the United States today. We can want it to be done, but that's just not possible to make that happen overnight," said Trent Emeneker, who previously led the Blue UAS Project, the Pentagon program responsible for vetting secure drones and parts.
"Anything that can be done to build the supply chain up outside of that mainland Chinese ecosystem, it's a good thing," said Emeneker, who runs a drone-training startup, Kill Zone.

Taiwan's government spurred a gold rush in August when it allocated over $7 billion to spend on drones over the next six years, driving new deals and breathing life into partnerships that were established when the budget was still on the horizon.
Officials in Taiwan see establishing a full-fledged domestic drone industry as vital to deterring China from using force to try to seize the island, which it considers to be its territory.

The urgency has grown as President Trump withholds approval for the sale of $14 billion in arms to Taiwan. Supporters see defense-industry collaboration as a way to strengthen ties between Washington and Taipei, amid worries that the U.S. is no longer willing or able to help the island defend itself.
Tech plus industry
The partnership strategy emulates the "you design it, we'll build it" model championed by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the powerhouse of the island's economic growth.

Taiwan was transformed into a global manufacturing hub in the 1970s, well before it became known as the source of the world's semiconductors. Over the decades, it has built a reputation as a nimble contract manufacturer supported by a network of local industries.

"American companies are already coming to Taiwan to find R&D partners and build out their drone supply chains," Raymond Greene, director of the American Institute in Taiwan, the de facto U.S. embassy, said in a speech this summer.

Chen Jeng-horng, chairman of Taiwan's largest shipbuilder, CSBC, witnessed the rush of Western startups after Taiwan's Defense Ministry said in December that it needed 1,320 one-way surface drones — uncrewed attack boats that blow up when they reach their target. The navy later requested $930 million over a six-year period to buy them.

CSBC, which has built warships for Taiwan for more than five decades and is building the island's first submarine, has been inundated with potential collaborators offering drone technology and in need of shipbuilding know-how.
"American firms are all flocking to us," Chen said at the company's Taipei office. "If they want to expand their business, Taiwan is the next major client."
While Taiwan has a strong industrial base and excels at shipbuilding, it lacks the technology to remotely control a large number of uncrewed systems across land, sea and air, Chen said.

Chen and other CSBC executives spent more than half a year vetting about a dozen U.S. and European firms for partnerships to compete for the navy's drone-boat contract. They toured the U.S., checked out product demos at sea and met with executives, ultimately picking HavocAI. Chen flew to Rhode Island last month to sign the deal.
Avoiding China
Such partnerships represent progress in building a so-called "non-red" or "democratic" supply chain that can serve both Taiwan and the Pentagon.
Most parts that Taiwanese vendors are making for Anduril are for products not made for use in Taiwan, said Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey.

"My business interest is maybe 'designed in the U.S., made in Taiwan,' or 'designed collaboratively and made in Taiwan,'" Luckey said in a small group interview in Taipei. But Taiwan "needs to design its own weapons systems and manufacture its own weapons systems at scale" to face Chinese threats, he said.

The National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, the R&D arm of the Taiwanese military, signed a co-production deal last year with Anduril to manufacture the U.S. company's Barracuda 500 cruise missiles and underwater drones in Taiwan.

It was one of six agreements NCSIST signed the same day with Western companies, including a plan with Northrop Grumman to explore collaboration on air and missile defense modernization for Taiwan's Defense Ministry.
At the end of last year, Congress directed the Pentagon to establish a joint drone program with Taiwan.
"The longer-term U.S.-Taiwan collaboration may have significant benefits to American defenses," said Rupert Hammond-Chambers, president of the U.S.-Taiwan Business Council.

The partnerships could also potentially supply U.S. forces overseas. This could be particularly valuable for U.S. Pacific Command, which operates thousands of miles from the American mainland, where "Taiwanese production can fill a need that does exist," said Emeneker.
Proving ground

Another potential contender for the Taiwan navy's proposed $930 million drone-boat budget is Str8 Industries, a startup co-founded by tech entrepreneur Phil Ho and Bilal Awad, a retired U.S. Navy officer.
Str8 is pitching itself as a company that can "build capabilities in situ — in Taiwan for the potential contingency scenarios," said Ho, referring to the possibility of a Chinese attack.
Str8 has an R&D operation in northern Taiwan, works with a shipyard in the southern Taiwan port of Kaohsiung and has a home office in Virginia, said Ho.
If China blockades Taiwan, Ho said, "everything on the island is what you can rely on."

In late September, the fruits of another U.S.-Taiwan partnership were on display in a live demonstration on Taiwan's southeastern coast. A small, white fixed-wing drone built by California-based AEVEX and Taiwan's CIRC took off from an airstrip and very quickly descended to strike a target on the ground — a red balloon.

AEVEX, which is already a Pentagon supplier, provided the design for the Taiwan-made, 3-D-printed airframe. CIRC designed the flight controller, computing board and payload systems, and sourced motors and batteries locally.
